familiar: I felt happy to see a familiar face at my new school.
Is this street familiar to you, or have we never been here?
Everything in my gran's house feels warm and familiar.
temperature: Use the thermometer to read the temperature of the classroom.
What temperature should the oven be for baking this cake?
Ice cubes melt when the temperature goes above freezing.
signature: Mum wrote her signature at the bottom of the school letter.
Can you read the swirly signature on this birthday card?
The delivery driver asked for a signature when the parcel came.
persuade: Nothing could persuade the cat to come out from under the bed.
Mum tried to persuade me to eat my peas.
How will you persuade the class to play your game at break time?
curiosity: Her curiosity about the stars made her ask lots of questions at bedtime.
The kitten's curiosity grew when it saw the open cupboard.
With great curiosity, we watched the snail slide up the wall.
average: It was just an average day, with nothing special at school.
The film was only average, so we felt a bit bored.
The average mark in our spelling test was seven out of ten.
develop: Tadpoles slowly develop legs and turn into frogs.
Practise every day and your football skills will develop.
I want to develop my story by adding a funny ending.
environment: Picking up litter helps keep our environment clean and tidy.
Penguins live in a cold environment full of ice and snow.
Why is it important to care for the environment around our school?
shoulder: My little cousin fell asleep on my shoulder in the car.
I tapped my friend on the shoulder to say hello.
Which shoulder do you use to hold your school bag?
achieve: If you practise every day, you can achieve your goal.
Did our class achieve its target of reading fifty books?
I will keep trying until I achieve a perfect score in the quiz.

rejected.s: The author wrote her signature inside my new library book.
rejected.reason: checker: An author signing a library book is odd, because library books are shared, so the setting is muddled.

rejected.s: I will try to persuade Dad to let us get a puppy.
rejected.reason: machine rule 4: capital word not allowed: Dad

rejected.s: What a lot of curiosity you have about how clocks work!
rejected.reason: checker: 'What a lot of curiosity you have' is awkward, unnatural English.

rejected.s: Is my sister taller than the average girl in her class?
rejected.reason: checker: Comparing a child's height is body talk, so we drop it.

rejected.s: How do butterflies develop inside their cocoons?
rejected.reason: checker: Butterflies develop in a chrysalis, not a cocoon, so the fact is wrong.

rejected.s: What do you hope to achieve in the art lesson this term?
rejected.reason: checker: 'What do you hope to develop in the art lesson' also makes sense. (also fits: develop)

rejected.s: It takes patience to achieve a tall tower of blocks!
rejected.reason: reader flag odd (Achieve sounds strange with 'a tall tower of blocks'; you would normally say build a tower.); re-judge: The flag is right. 'Achieve' normally goes with goals, results or success (achieve a goal, achieve your best), not with a physical object like a tower. Children would naturally say 'build a tower', so 'build' fits the gap better than the target word. That makes the sentence a poor model of how 'achieve' is used and leaves the answer unclear.

rejected.s: If you practise your spelling every night, you will achieve full marks.
rejected.reason: machine rule 6: too like another candidate

rejected.s: After many weeks of trying, we could finally achieve our aim of a tidy garden!
We worked as a team to achieve a tidy classroom.
rejected.reason: checker: 'Achieve a tidy classroom' sounds a little odd and could tempt a child to try develop, so it is dropped.

rejected.s: Mum says patience and hard work help you achieve almost anything!
rejected.reason: checker: 'Help you shoulder almost anything' also makes sense, so the gap has more than one answer. (also fits: shoulder)
